subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
'Chetan? Sorry, can I ask something stupid?'
'Probably not stupid. Go on, Leela.'
'In the stand-up, what's a "blocker"? Everyone kept saying it.'
'Anything stopping your work. Like if you're waiting on someone else's code.'
'Oh. Okay.' Leela let out a breath and pushed her hair back. 'I thought everyone just knew these things.'
Chetan laughed. 'A year ago I sat exactly where you're sitting. I thought "sprint" meant we had to physically run somewhere.'
'You?'
'Me. And last week I didn't know what a "feature flag" was. Asked Anirudh. Still not sure I get it fully.' He shrugged. 'You don't stop not-knowing things here. You just stop being scared of it.'
Leela smiled. 'Can I keep asking you?'
'Please. Someone asked me a hundred questions my first month. It's my turn.' He pulled over a chair. 'Show me your first ticket. We'll do it together.'

qa.q: What does 'blocker' mean, according to Chetan?
qa.a: Anything stopping your work, like waiting on someone else's code.

qa.q: What does Leela's long breath suggest about how she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests relief, since she had worried that everyone else already knew these things and she didn't.

qa.q: How does Chetan's attitude help both Leela and himself?
qa.a: He admits he still doesn't know everything and helps her openly, which makes her feel safe and deepens his own sense of belonging on the team.

qa.q: How might Leela see Chetan after hearing about 'sprint'?
qa.a: She may see him as approachable rather than intimidating, and feel her own confusion is normal.

grounding: It shows a person whose confidence has grown accepting that not knowing is normal and helping a newcomer, which strengthens his sense of belonging.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
It's odd. Eighteen months ago I was the one hiding in the staff room at the school, sure the principal had hired me by accident. Now I'm the one the new teachers are sent to.
This term it's Akash, twenty-three, straight from his B.Ed. On his second day he asked me, very quietly, how to fill in the attendance register, as if it were a secret. I laughed, kindly I hope, and told him I'd filled mine in wrong for the whole of my first month.
I don't know everything. Last week I had to ask the librarian how the new book-issue system works. I just ask now, without the old dread.
Helping Akash, I keep remembering my own first term, the chalk dust, the stomach aches. I feel fond of that version of me.
When he thanked me yesterday, I felt, for the first time, that I really belong here.
— Jahnavi

qa.q: What did Akash ask Jahnavi on his second day?
qa.a: He asked how to fill in the attendance register.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel now when remembering the first term?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels fond and a little nostalgic about that earlier, scared version of self.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's way of handling not knowing show about mature confidence?
qa.a: It shows that asking plainly, like asking the librarian, is normal, and that confidence can grow without pretending to know everything.

qa.q: How might Akash feel hearing that Jahnavi filled the register in wrong for a month?
qa.a: Akash may feel relieved and less ashamed, and more willing to ask further questions.

grounding: It shows a teacher whose confidence has grown with competence, who accepts not knowing everything and helps the next newcomer, cementing belonging.
